title: Marketing Science Readiness Score
subtitle: Measures how much of your marketing activity, brand story, and positioning signals are doing traceable, revenue-linked work.

questions.text: How recently have you tested what AI tools say about your company when a buyer asks them to compare options in your space?

answers.label: I have never done this
I did it once, more than a year ago
I have done it a few times but not systematically
I did it in the last six months and documented the results
I run this test regularly and act on the findings

questions.text: If you asked three different AI tools to describe your company today, how consistent would those descriptions be?

answers.label: I genuinely have no idea
Probably inconsistent; I have not shaped what they pull from
Somewhat consistent on the basics, but the framing likely varies
Fairly consistent because we have published clear, structured positioning
Consistently accurate; I have tested and validated the outputs

questions.text: Do you have a structured document that defines exactly how your company should be described, written so AI models can find it and pull from it?

answers.label: No structured document exists
There is an About page but nothing built for machine readability
We have a brand guide but it was not designed with AI citation in mind
We have structured content specifically designed for this purpose
Yes, and we update it based on what AI tools are actually pulling

low.headline: You are invisible where buyers are now doing research.
low.text: AI tools described the same B2B company in contradictory ways 28% of the time in our research. If you have not tested what AI says about yours, you do not know whether buyers are getting accurate information or a garbled version of your positioning when they compare options.
steps: Run a prompt test this week: ask ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini to describe your company and the problems you solve. Screenshot all three outputs.
Compare those descriptions against your own positioning and mark every contradiction.
Create one structured brand-signal document, a clear machine-readable page that defines who you are, who you serve, and what outcomes you produce.

mid.headline: You have a foundation. Now you need to close the consistency gap.
mid.text: You are aware this matters and you have taken some steps. But inconsistency at the AI layer still costs you citations when buyers compare vendors. The structural change is not a one-time fix; it is a system that needs to run on a schedule.
steps: Schedule a quarterly AI audit: test three to five tools, compare outputs, and identify which brand signals are landing and which are not.
Publish structured case studies and positioning statements in formats AI crawlers can parse easily.
Review which claims about your company appear most often and verify they match your current positioning, not where you were two years ago.

high.headline: You are building the structural advantage most brands have not figured out yet.
high.text: Consistent AI citation is a buying-stage advantage, not a vanity metric. You have done the work to get here. The next move is treating it as a living signal, not a one-time project.
steps: Document your audit methodology so the process survives personnel changes.
Look for the gaps: which sub-topics in your space is AI citing you for least? Those are your next content targets.
Track whether your citation rate improves after publishing new structured content, and close the feedback loop.

questions.text: When you trace your brand story back to its source, is it built on something your product or service actually does in your customer's daily work or life?

answers.label: Our story is mostly about what we believe, not what we do for people
There is a functional truth in there but it is not the center of the story
The functional truth is present but buried under brand language
The story is grounded in what we do for clients, with specific examples
Our story makes our function literal and specific, not aspirational

questions.text: How often does your best marketing insight come from what a client explains and then immediately dismisses as too obvious to mention?

answers.label: I do not have a process for finding that; I start with what I want to say
Occasionally, but not by design
Sometimes; I know to listen for it but the results are inconsistent
Often; client conversations regularly surface the real story
Always; our discovery process is specifically designed to find it

questions.text: Would someone who scrolled past your content know specifically what you do for clients, or would they come away with a feeling and no details?

answers.label: A feeling only; we lead with values and aspiration
Mostly a feeling, with occasional specifics
A mix; some content is concrete, some is atmospheric
Mostly concrete; a reader could describe what we do and for whom
Concrete and specific; our content does a job, not decoration

low.headline: Your story is decoration. People scroll past decoration.
low.text: A story that is not built to do real work is not marketing. The Crocs team did not pitch the shoe; they made literal what the shoe already does in a customer's life. That is the difference between a campaign people share and one that runs its budget out quietly.
steps: Pull your last five pieces of content. For each one, write one sentence on the specific job it does for the reader. If you cannot write it, that piece is decoration.
Schedule a 30-minute client conversation with one goal: find the thing they almost do not mention because it feels obvious. That is your next brief.
Rewrite your current homepage headline so a stranger could describe your business after reading it, without clicking anything.

mid.headline: The functional truth is in there. It needs to move to the center.
mid.text: You have real material to work with. The gap is that it is buried under language that sounds like marketing rather than what actually happens for clients. Bring the specific thing forward and let the aspiration follow from it.
steps: Identify the one outcome clients describe most specifically when they explain why they hired you. Lead with that.
Audit your discovery process: are you starting with what you want to say, or are you listening for what they keep coming back to?
For your next content piece, reverse the order: start with a client detail that felt almost too small to mention, then build out from there.

high.headline: Your content is doing work. Now systematize how you find it.
high.text: You have built the habit of grounding your story in functional truth. The next question is whether you can produce it consistently, not just when the right client conversation happens to surface it.
steps: Document the discovery questions that reliably surface the too-obvious-to-mention insight. Build them into every client intake.
Audit your content mix quarterly: what percentage is grounded in specific client function versus general belief statements?
Push further into the specific; the more concrete the detail, the less it looks like content and the more it looks like evidence.

questions.text: If I asked you right now which three marketing activities drove the most revenue last quarter, how quickly could you answer?

answers.label: I could not; we do not track it at that level
I would have a guess but no data to back it up
I could name the activities but not quantify their contribution
I could answer with reasonable confidence based on our tracking
I could answer in under two minutes with specific numbers

questions.text: When you decide what to stop funding, how much of that decision is driven by data versus instinct or budget pressure?

answers.label: Almost entirely instinct or whatever stopped feeling important
Mostly instinct, occasionally backed by a number
A mix; we have some data but the decision is still mostly judgment
Mostly data; we have clear performance criteria before we cut anything
Data-first; nothing gets cut without a measurable reason, and nothing continues without one either

questions.text: Out of all the marketing activities you ran last quarter, what percentage can you directly tie to a measurable revenue outcome?
questions.hint: Count only activities where you can trace a clear line: this activity produced this response, which led to this deal or pipeline event. Be conservative.

questions.text: How many hours per week does your team spend on marketing execution — content, campaigns, outreach, and reporting combined?
questions.hint: Include your own time if you run marketing. Count all hands-on execution hours, not planning or strategy time.

low.headline: You are funding activities you cannot defend.
low.text: If you cannot trace your marketing spend to revenue outcomes, you are not running a marketing function — you are running on assumption. That is a solvable problem, but you have to be willing to name which activities have no accountability and stop protecting them.
steps: List every marketing activity from last quarter. Next to each one, write the revenue signal it is supposed to generate. If you cannot write it, that activity has no accountability.
Pick your three highest-cost activities and ask: what would change in our pipeline if we stopped this tomorrow? If the honest answer is not much, stop it.
Set up one tracking mechanism, even a simple spreadsheet, that connects marketing activities to pipeline events before you run another campaign.

mid.headline: You have partial visibility. Partial visibility still funds the wrong things.
mid.text: You know which activities work in the areas you have measured. The gap is what is running outside your measurement window. That is where budget disappears without leaving a trace.
steps: Map the exact boundaries of your current tracking: what gets measured, what does not, and what the gap costs you in hours and spend.
For every activity outside your tracking window, set a 90-day test with a defined outcome threshold before the test starts.
Review your marketing spend quarterly with one question: which of these has earned the right to continue?

high.headline: You are running marketing the way it should be run. Protect the rigor.
high.text: Revenue-linked decision making is the thing most marketing teams say they have and do not. You have it. The risk at this stage is drift; adding activities without accountability as the team or budget grows.
steps: Codify your attribution model so it survives adding headcount or changing tools.
Check whether your tracking catches lagging signals; some activities produce revenue 90 days out, and those should not get cut prematurely.
Use your attribution data to make the business case for the next marketing investment. That is the compounding advantage.

questions.text: In the last year, can you name a period where you made decisions that did not show up in the numbers right away but changed what you were capable of six months later?

answers.label: No; we only fund things with near-term measurable return
Maybe; I can name a period but I am not sure it was intentional
Yes; I can name it, but I could not explain the criteria that made it worth holding
Yes; I made a deliberate investment and tracked whether it paid off
Yes; I have a framework for distinguishing investment periods from problem periods

questions.text: When you have a slow quarter, how do you tell whether it is a problem to solve or an investment period that will pay off later?

answers.label: I treat every slow quarter as a problem and try to fix it fast
Gut feel; I cannot always explain why I make the call I make
I have some indicators but they are informal and inconsistent
I have a set of signals I review deliberately before making the call
I have written criteria and review whether I was right after the fact

questions.text: How confident are you that your current marketing investment mix balances near-term pipeline work with longer-term brand-signal building?

answers.label: Not confident; almost everything is near-term and reactive
Slightly confident; we have some longer-term work but it is underfunded
Somewhat confident; the mix feels about right but it is not based on a model
Confident; we have made deliberate allocations with a rationale for each
Very confident; we revisit the allocation quarterly and adjust based on what we are seeing

low.headline: You are optimizing for the month you are in and shortchanging the business you could have.
low.text: A step back and a step to the side can look almost identical from the outside. The investment periods you cut short are the ones you never get back. Some of the biggest forward moves in a business come after months that looked, from the outside, like nothing was happening.
steps: Name the last time you made a decision that did not pay off for at least 90 days. What made you hold it? If you cannot name one, that is the gap.
Separate your marketing activities into two lists: pipeline now versus capability in six months. If the second list is empty, you are underinvesting in your next quarter.
Before your next planning cycle, write what you are building toward in six months, then work back to the investments that get you there.

mid.headline: You understand the distinction. You need criteria, not instinct.
mid.text: Knowing that a step to the side is different from a step back is a start. Acting on it consistently requires a defined set of signals to review before you decide, not a feel that shifts with the news in your pipeline that week.
steps: Write down the signals you would look for to tell you a slow period is an investment and not a problem. Review those signals the next time you are tempted to pull back.
Pick one activity you have been running on faith and define what a successful outcome looks like in 90 days. If it does not hit, cut it. If it does, fund it more.
Build a simple review into your quarterly planning: for each longer-term investment, write whether it delivered and what you would do differently.

high.headline: You have the strategic clarity most marketing leaders do not build until it is too late.
high.text: Being able to distinguish investment from problem — and hold the investment periods when external pressure to cut is high — is one of the hardest things in marketing leadership. You are doing it. Now the work is to document how, so it does not live only in your head.
steps: Write down your decision criteria for distinguishing a step back from a step to the side. Make it transferable to your team.
Review your last three major investment periods: did they pay off on the timeline you expected? What does that tell you about your calibration?
Use your track record to build conviction when you defend future investment periods to stakeholders who only see the slow month.

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: In 30 minutes I'll show you which two gaps to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing.
